title: Lecha Dodi
description: Lecha Dodi ("Come, my beloved"), the Friday-night hymn that greets the Sabbath as a bride, sung in Hebrew to the old Ashkenazi melody kept for the weeks of the Omer, for 2 to 4 singers. The refrain says: come, my beloved, to meet the bride, let us welcome the Sabbath; the first verse tells that "keep" and "remember" were spoken in one word by the one God, and the last welcomes the Sabbath, her husband's crown, in peace and joy.

credits.tune: traditional Ashkenazi melody for the Omer weeks (printed by Francis L. Cohen, 1904)

licence.words: public domain: Hebrew hymn by Solomon ha-Levi Alkabetz (16th century)
licence.tune: public domain: traditional, printed by Francis L. Cohen in The Jewish Encyclopedia, vol. 7 (1904); Cohen died 1934
licence.arrangement: original, written for Stackapella (the print is a melody only)
licence.source: melody from The Jewish Encyclopedia, vol. 7 (New York and London: Funk and Wagnalls, 1904), pp. 675 to 677, article "Lekah Dodi" by Cyrus Adler and Francis L. Cohen (Adler died 1940, Cohen 1934), the music example "Lekah Dodi (Melody for 'Omer Weeks)", p. 677, Andantino, G major, 3/4, a pickup and a 16-bar verse with an 8-bar refrain, printed with an English verse ("How lovely is the Day of Rest, Rich source of blessing, welcome guest", a rendering of the hymn's second stanza) and an English refrain ("Then come, my friend, to meet the Bride"); written here in G as printed. The other tunes in the article (the Three Weeks tune and the Moorish chant, pp. 676 to 677) are not used. The Hebrew is fitted by us in modern Israeli pronunciation: the refrain sung first, as the hymn is sung, then after each verse; verses 1 ("Shamor vezachor") and 9 ("Bo'i veshalom", with "berina", the Sabbath reading of the Nusach Sefard (Hasidic) prayer books; Ashkenazi prayer books have "besimcha", on the same notes). The refrain fits the printed refrain syllable for syllable, its stresses (CHA, RAT, LA, NEI, BAT, LA) on downbeats; the Hebrew verses need more syllables than the English, so some printed half notes are sung as two quarters on the same pitch and some slurred pairs carry two syllables (the pitches unchanged), and verse 1's "A-do-" splits the pickup into two eighths. Divine names in the substituted forms sung outside prayer: "Kel" for El and "Adoshem" for the four-letter name (on the same notes). Breaths written in for beginners: each line's last half note gives up three quarters of a beat, and in the refrain's middle the slurred "la" gives up half a beat and the pickup "pe-" starts a quarter later.
